name: Superior colliculus
function: Multimodal orienting center of the tectum: builds a retinotopic and spatiotopic map on which salient visual (and auditory/somatosensory) stimuli trigger saccades and combined eye-head turning; also relays visual reflexes such as the pupillary light reflex through its rostral pretectal neighbors. Its output gates orienting movement via tectospinal and tectobulbar projections.

afferent: Retina (direct retinotectal fibers and via the optic tract)
Striate and extrastriate visual cortex (corticotectal fibers)
Substantia nigra, pars reticulata (tonic GABAergic gating)
efferent: Tectospinal tract (crosses in the dorsal tegmental decussation to contralateral neck/upper cord)
Tectobulbar fibers to the PPRF and CN III/IV/VI nuclei for saccade initiation

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery; lateral portion also receives branches of the superior cerebellar artery

clinical.findings: Dorsal midbrain compression or infarction involving the superior colliculus/pretectal region impairs vertical saccades and the pupillary light reflex (light-near dissociation).
clinical.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA; pineal region mass effect

clinical.findings: Experimental collicular lesions impair initiation of reflexive saccades toward peripheral targets and visual attention shifting, while voluntary scanning is relatively preserved (cortical saccade generation is intact).
clinical.note: Rarely isolated in humans; derived mainly from lesion and stimulation studies.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control" (supranuclear control of eye movements)
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Inferior colliculus
function: Obligatory integrative relay of the central auditory pathway: nearly all ascending auditory fibers converge here in a tonotopic map that preserves binaural timing- and intensity-based sound localization cues, before output continues through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus. Also participates in auditory startle and orienting responses.

afferent: Lateral lemniscus (from cochlear nuclei and superior olivary complex)
Contralateral inferior colliculus (commissure of the inferior colliculus)
efferent: Brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)
Commissural fibers to the contralateral inferior colliculus
Superior colliculus and reticular formation (auditory orienting/startle)

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery; caudal branches of the superior cerebellar artery

clinical.findings: Small lesions of the inferior colliculus degrade sound localization and hearing quality without causing unilateral deafness, because auditory pathways are bilaterally represented at and above this level.
clinical.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA or SCA

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Pretectal area
function: Pretectal interneurons receive retinal input and bilaterally drive the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to constrict both pupils in the light reflex; they coordinate the pupillary component of the near response and interface with the vertical gaze centers of the rostral midbrain.

afferent: Retina via the optic tract (brachium of the superior colliculus region)
efferent: Bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei (partly crossing through the posterior commissure)

bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Pretectal destruction abolishes the pupillary light reflex while sparing accommodation, producing large pupils that 'accommodate but do not react' together with vertical gaze palsy and convergence-retraction nystagmus.
clinical.vascular: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA; pineal region mass effect

clinical.findings: Selective pretectal-to-EW light-reflex interruption (classically neurosyphilis) yields small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light.
clinical.note: Contrast with Adie pupil, which is a lesion of the ciliary ganglion beyond the EW neurons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control" (pupillary abnormalities)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Periaqueductal gray
function: Central hub of endogenous pain modulation: the PAG is densely packed with mu-opioid receptors, and stimulation releases endogenous opioids that activate a descending analgesia pathway (PAG to rostral ventromedial medulla and locus coeruleus-side noradrenergic systems to the dorsal horn). It also organizes autonomic and behavioral responses to threat and stress, including fight-or-flight cardiovascular changes, defensive behavior, micturition, and vocalization.

efferent: Nucleus raphe magnus and medullary reticular formation (descending analgesia)
Hypothalamus and brainstem autonomic nuclei (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor vagal nucleus)

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip and proximal posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating territory); collicular branches dorsally

clinical.syndrome: Central poststroke pain and opioid analgesia
clinical.findings: PAG involvement in paramedian midbrain infarcts can contribute to central neuropathic pain and blunted endogenous opioid analgesia; conversely, deep-brain stimulation of the PAG is an established therapy for refractory pain.
clinical.vascular: Paramedian perforators of the basilar tip/PCA
clinical.note: The PAG is a classic stimulation target for intractable cancer and deafferentation pain.

clinical.findings: PAG activation coordinates stress hypergravity responses: tachycardia, hypertension, hyperventilation, and defensive freezing or flight behavior.
clinical.note: Functional-imaging correlate of threat processing; discrete human lesions are rare.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Nolte, The Human Brain: An Introduction to Its Functional Anatomy — midbrain and pain-modulation sections
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Oculomotor nucleus (CN III)
function: Somatic motor complex innervating the medial, superior, and inferior rectus, the inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris via CN III; arranged as paired subnuclei plus a single midline central caudal (levator) column. Each subnucleus supplies contralateral target muscles except the superior rectus, so nuclear lesions can produce bilateral ptosis with asymmetric ophthalmoparesis.

afferent: Medial longitudinal fasciculus from contralateral abducens internuclear neurons (conjugate horizontal gaze)
Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal (vertical gaze holding)
efferent: CN III fascicles running ventrally through the red nucleus to exit in the interpeduncular fossa
Extraocular muscles (medial/superior/inferior rectus, inferior oblique) and levator palpebrae

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery (posterior thalamoperforating); the exiting nerve passes between PCA and SCA

clinical.findings: Fascicular CN III palsy (ipsilateral ptosis, mydriasis, 'down and out' eye) combined with contralateral hemiplegia of face, arm, and leg from crus cerebri involvement.
clinical.vascular: Paramedian branches of the PCA (posterior thalamoperforating)

clinical.findings: Compressive lesions (classically posterior communicating artery aneurysm) at the fascicle or nerve produce mydriasis with ptosis and ophthalmoparesis; parasympathetic fibers run peripherally in the nerve, so pupillary involvement signals compression and demands emergency imaging.
clinical.vascular: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm; PCA/SCA interval infarct (pupil-sparing, microvascular)

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control" (extraocular muscles, nerves, and nuclei)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Edinger-Westphal nucleus
function: Parasympathetic preganglionic (visceral oculomotor) nucleus dorsal to the oculomotor complex: its preganglionic fibers travel with CN III to the ciliary ganglion, where postganglionic fibers excite the sphincter pupillae (miosis) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation).

afferent: Pretectal area (bilateral light-reflex interneurons, partly via the posterior commissure)
Medial rectus subnucleus / supranuclear near-response input
efferent: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in CN III to the ciliary ganglion
Postganglionic short ciliary nerves to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) and severe diabetic/autonomic lesions interrupt the pretectal input to the EW nucleus so the pupil accommodates but does not constrict to light.
clinical.vascular: Paramedian PCA perforators; also seen with large-fiber diabetic autonomic neuropathy (afferent/efferent pupillary fibers)

clinical.findings: Fascicular or peripheral CN III lesions that sweep the EW-derived parasympathetic fibers produce a dilated, poorly reactive pupil with ptosis and diplopia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control" (the pupils and other ocular autonomic pathways)
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Trochlear nucleus (CN IV)
function: Innervates the contralateral superior oblique muscle via CN IV, which depresses, intorts, and abducts the globe. CN IV is unique: its fibers curve dorsally around the cerebral aqueduct, decussate completely in the superior medullary velum, and exit the dorsal midbrain just below the inferior colliculus — the only cranial nerve with a fully crossed intramedullary course and a dorsal exit.

afferent: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (vestibulo-ocular and internuclear input)
Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF (vertical saccade generation)
Cuneiform nucleus and mesencephalic reticular formation
efferent: CN IV fibers around the aqueduct decussating in the superior medullary velum

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Vertical diplopia worst on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral head tilt (Bielschowsky head-tilt test); patients tilt the head away from the paretic side. Common causes: closed head trauma at the dorsal exit/decussation and microvascular ischemia.
clinical.vascular: Paramedian perforators; long subarachnoid course makes the nerve vulnerable to tentorial-edge trauma

clinical.findings: Bilateral dorsal exit/decussation injury produces a 'V-pattern' esotropia with large excyclotorsion — a classic sequela of severe closed head injury.
clinical.vascular: Collicular/SCA branches at the dorsal midbrain

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cranial Nerves" (CN IV course)
Patten, Neurological Differential Diagnosis — midbrain level plates

name: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus
function: A column of pseudounipolar primary sensory neurons embedded within the CNS — the only such group in the brain: these cells are the proprioceptive ganglion for the masticatory muscles and periodontal ligament, conveying jaw position and bite-force information and serving as the afferent limb of the monosynaptic jaw-jerk reflex. Extends from the rostral pons through the midbrain.

afferent: Ia muscle-spindle and periodontal afferents of CN V that bypass the trigeminal ganglion and descend via the mesencephalic tract
efferent: Monosynaptic collateral to the trigeminal motor nucleus (jaw-jerk reflex arc)
Cerebellar connections via the superior cerebellar peduncle region

bloodSupply: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery (dorsolateral tegmentum); paramedian perforators medially

clinical.findings: Because the mesencephalic nucleus provides the afferent limb, bilateral corticobulbar (pseudobulbar) disease releases the jaw-jerk reflex, which becomes brisk — a sign of upper motor neuron involvement above the trigeminal motor nucleus.
clinical.note: Isolated lesions of the nucleus are clinically silent; assessed as part of the CN V examination.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply" (cranial nerve nuclei and related structures)
Snell, Clinical Neuroanatomy — brainstem sections (trigeminal system)

name: Mesencephalic trigeminal tract
function: Slender fiber bundle running along the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray through the dorsolateral midbrain and rostral pons, carrying the central processes and reflex collaterals of the mesencephalic trigeminal neurons — the afferent limb of the jaw-jerk reflex.

afferent: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus neuron processes (jaw proprioception)

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery branches (dorsolateral tegmentum)

clinical.findings: Isolated involvement is asymptomatic; damage together with the mesencephalic nucleus blunts jaw position sense and alters the jaw-jerk reflex.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Red nucleus
function: Relay of the lateral (cerebellar) motor system in the rostral midbrain tegmentum. The caudal magnocellular part is the origin of the rubrospinal tract, which crosses immediately in the ventral tegmentum and facilitates flexor tone of the contralateral limbs; the rostral parvocellular part links the cerebellum with the inferior olive through the central tegmental tract (rubro-olivary, Guillain-Mollaret loop) and subserves motor learning. In humans the rubrospinal system is vestigial relative to the corticospinal tract, but the nucleus remains a major dentatorubrothalamic relay.

afferent: Contralateral dentate and interposed nuclei (via the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation)
efferent: Rubrospinal tract (decussates ventromedially at this level)
Central tegmental tract to the ipsilateral inferior olivary nucleus

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the basilar tip / PCA (medial red nucleus); branches of the superior cerebellar artery (lateral)

clinical.findings: Ventral tegmental lesion of CN III fascicles plus the red nucleus: ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral tremor, choreoathetosis, or ataxia.
More dorsal tegmental lesion combining CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia from red nucleus and dentatorubrothalamic (SCP) fiber involvement.
Lesions of the red nucleus or its dentatorubral input produce a low-frequency (2-4.5 Hz) rest-and-postural tremor, sometimes appearing weeks to months after the injury.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Corticospinal Tract and Other Motor Pathways" (rubrospinal tract)
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Substantia nigra, pars compacta
function: Melanin-pigmented dopaminergic nucleus forming the dorsal band of the substantia nigra: its nigrostriatal projection to the caudate and putamen facilitates the direct (movement-facilitating) basal ganglia pathway, while mesocortical and mesolimbic projections modulate cognition and reward. Progressive degeneration of SNc neurons with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, depleting striatal dopamine, produces Parkinson's disease.

efferent: Nigrostriatal dopaminergic fibers to the caudate/putamen
Mesolimbic fibers to the nucleus accumbens

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the posterior cerebral artery; anterior choroidal artery branches (lateral/caudal portions)

clinical.findings: Loss of more than half of SNc dopaminergic neurons with striatal dopamine depletion produces the cardinal tetrad: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability.
Infarcts or hemorrhages involving the substantia nigra cause contralateral parkinsonism or hemiparkinsonism, and acute nigral lesions may add hemiballistic or dystonic movements.
clinical.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Basal Ganglia" (Parkinson's disease and related disorders)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy — basal ganglia and brainstem sections

name: Substantia nigra, pars reticulata
function: One of the two GABAergic output nuclei of the basal ganglia (with the internal globus pallidus): SNr neurons fire tonically and tonically inhibit the superior colliculus and thalamus. Corticostriatal excitation of the direct pathway inhibits the SNr, disinhibiting collicular saccade circuits and thalamocortical motor loops; the indirect pathway (via the subthalamic nucleus) increases SNr output and suppresses movement.
bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the PCA; anterior choroidal artery branches laterally

clinical.findings: SNr infarcts or hemorrhages disinhibit thalamic and collicular targets, producing contralateral dystonia, chorea, or hemiballism-like involuntary movements.
clinical.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery

clinical.findings: SNr neurons fire tonically and hold the superior colliculus under GABAergic inhibition, so loss of nigral output removes the brake on reflexive visually guided saccades: patients make unwanted, short-latency saccades towards novel stimuli and are visually distractible, a pattern also described in progressive supranuclear palsy, in which SNr cell loss is a pathological hallmark.
clinical.vascular: PCA paramedian perforators; anterior choroidal artery
clinical.note: The mirror image of Parkinson's disease: here the dopaminergic pars compacta is spared while the GABAergic output nucleus fails, so the picture is hyperkinetic and saccade-happy rather than bradykinetic.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Basal Ganglia"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Crus cerebri
function: Ventral midbrain fiber bundle (basis pedunculi) carrying all descending corticofugal fibers with strict medial-to-lateral somatotopy: frontopontine fibers most medial, then corticobulbar fibers, then corticospinal fibers, and temporoparietooccipitopontine fibers most lateral. Rostrally continuous with the internal capsule; caudally it disperses into the longitudinal fasciculi of the basis pontis and re-forms as the medullary pyramids.

afferent: Internal capsule (genu and posterior limb): corticobulbar, corticospinal, and corticopontine fibers
efferent: Basis pontis (corticopontine fibers synapse in pontine nuclei)
Medullary pyramids (corticospinal continuation toward the pyramidal decussation)

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries; anterior choroidal artery (lateral crus)

clinical.findings: Medial crus infarction with CN III fascicles: ipsilateral pupil-involving CN III palsy plus contralateral face-arm-leg hemiplegia.
Any crus lesion paired with an ipsilateral third-nerve finding localizes the lesion to the ventral midbrain — the prototype of brainstem crossed syndromes (ipsilateral CN, contralateral body).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply" (long tracts)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Corticospinal Tract and Other Motor Pathways"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussation
synonyms: decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles
function: Ventral midline crossing of the superior cerebellar peduncles in the caudal midbrain tegmentum: virtually all dentatothalamocortical cerebellar output decussates here, so each cerebellar hemisphere ultimately coordinates the contralateral body through the red nucleus, VL/VA thalamus, and motor cortex.

afferent: Both superior cerebellar peduncles (dentate and interposed nucleus outflow)

bloodSupply: Paramedian perforators of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Paramedian lesions of the decussation interrupt cerebellar outflow producing limb ataxia and intention tremor; involvement of the adjacent oculomotor complex and MLF adds diplopia and gaze palsies.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Superior cerebellar peduncle
function: Principal efferent peduncle of the cerebellum: dentate and interposed nucleus fibers sweep rostrally through the dorsolateral pons and caudal midbrain, decussate completely in the ventral midbrain tegmentum, and reach the contralateral red nucleus and VL/VA thalamus (dentatorubrothalamic system). Because cerebellar output double-crosses, lesions here cause ipsilateral limb ataxia; chronic lesions may add contralateral dystonia.
bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery (pontine portion); paramedian perforators of the basilar tip (midbrain portion)

clinical.findings: SCP or dentate outflow lesions produce ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor, and limb ataxia; SCA-territory infarcts classically combine these with vertigo and nystagmus.
clinical.note: Adult-onset lesions may later develop contralateral (double-crossed) dystonia or choreoathetosis.

clinical.findings: Damage to the dentato-rubro-thalamic route at or above the peduncular decussation — the midbrain tegmentum, the red nucleus or the thalamic VL — leaves a coarse, slow (2-5 Hz) tremor of the contralateral limbs that is present at rest, worsens with posture and explodes on goal-directed movement, often with mild accompanying ataxia.
clinical.vascular: Superior cerebellar artery / paramedian basilar tip perforators
clinical.note: The delay of weeks to months between the stroke and the tremor, its contralateral side, and its partial response to levodopa or to VIM/subthalamic deep-brain stimulation separate it from acute cerebellar ataxia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Cerebellum"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Dorsal raphe nucleus
function: Largest of the rostral serotonergic (5-HT) raphe nuclei, lying midline between the MLFs ventral to the periaqueductal gray: it projects diffusely to the forebrain, diencephalon, and spinal cord, modulating sleep-wake cycling, mood, and nociception, and partners with the PAG in descending antinociception.

efferent: Diffuse serotonergic projections to cortex, striatum, thalamus, and hypothalamus

bloodSupply: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip / posterior cerebral artery

clinical.findings: Dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons are the principal pharmacological target of SSRIs; midbrain raphe involvement is associated with mood disturbance, sleep-wake disruption, and altered pain thresholds in brainstem disease.
clinical.note: Serotonergic dysfunction is documented pharmacologically and functionally rather than as a focal stroke syndrome.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply" (other functions of the brainstem: neurotransmitter modulation)
Nolte, The Human Brain: An Introduction to Its Functional Anatomy — reticular formation and monoaminergic systems

name: Cuneiform nucleus
function: Mesencephalic reticular formation of the dorsolateral tegmentum (with the adjacent pedunculopontine region forming the mesencephalic locomotor region): initiates and modulates gait and postural tone through descending reticulospinal systems, contributes to arousal via ascending projections to the intralaminar thalamus, and participates in pain modulation and startle.
bloodSupply: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery and collicular branches of the posterior cerebral artery (dorsolateral tegmentum)

clinical.syndrome: Gait ignition failure / freezing of gait
clinical.findings: The cuneiform-pedunculopontine mesencephalic locomotor region drives gait initiation; its degeneration or disconnection in parkinsonism contributes to freezing of gait and akinesia, and it is an investigational deep-brain-stimulation target.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply" (reticular formation)
Snell, Clinical Neuroanatomy — reticular formation sections

name: Interpeduncular fossa
function: Ventral midline recess between the two cerebral peduncles, roofed by the posterior perforated substance: CN III rootlets emerge into it, the basilar apex and posterior thalamoperforating vessels course around it, and the interpeduncular cistern fills it with CSF.
bloodSupply: Basilar apex (P1 segments and posterior thalamoperforators); posterior communicating artery branches

clinical.findings: Saccular aneurysms of the basilar apex within the interpeduncular cistern compress the CN III roots or midbrain, causing pupil-involving third-nerve palsy, altered consciousness, or top-of-the-basilar syndromes.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cranial Nerves" (surface features of the brainstem)
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) exit
synonyms: CN III rootlets in interpeduncular fossa
function: CN III rootlets emerge from the sulcus of the oculomotor nerve on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle into the interpeduncular fossa, then pass forward between the posterior cerebral artery (above) and the superior cerebellar artery (below) — the vascular interval where aneurysms compress the nerve and paramedian perforators infarct the fascicles (Weber territory).
bloodSupply: PCA/SCA interval perforators; recurrent branches of the posterior communicating artery to the nerve

clinical.findings: Ventral midbrain lesion at the exit zone: ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, mydriasis, down-and-out eye) with contralateral hemiplegia.
Aneurysm at the PCoA origin compresses the emerging nerve: acute painful pupil-involving third-nerve palsy — a neurosurgical emergency.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cranial Nerves" (skull foramina and cranial nerve exit points)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control"
RadioGraphics 2019, "Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes", doi:10.1148/rg.2019180126

name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) exit
synonyms: CN IV dorsal exit below inferior colliculus
function: Dorsal exit of CN IV: the trochlear fibers decussate completely within the superior (anterior) medullary velum and emerge from the dorsal midbrain just caudal to the inferior colliculi — the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem — then wrap around the cerebral peduncle for the longest intracranial subarachnoid course of any cranial nerve, entering the dura at the tentorial edge.
bloodSupply: Collicular (quadrigeminal) branches of the PCA; distal superior cerebellar artery branches

clinical.syndrome: Trochlear palsy after closed head trauma
clinical.findings: The long thin dorsal roots are stretched against the tentorial edge; bilateral trochlear palsies after trauma indicate exit/decussation-zone injury, with vertical diplopia worst on descending stairs or reading.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cranial Nerves" (CN IV course and exit)
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control"
